objectives: Distinguish evasion from poisoning from extraction attacks.
Recognize adversarial examples and their transferability.

slides.title: Three classes of attacks on ML systems
slides.body:
Machine learning models face a distinct threat landscape from classical software. **Battista Biggio** (University of Cagliari) was among the first to systematically study adversarial attacks on ML, publishing foundational work on poisoning (2012) and evasion (2013) years before the field's mainstream awakening — his 2013 paper "Evasion attacks against machine learning at test time" (Biggio et al., ECML-PKDD 2013) predates and parallels the better-known Szegedy et al. findings.

**Evasion attacks**: at inference time, craft an input that the model misclassifies. The canonical example is **adversarial examples** — demonstrated in "Intriguing properties of neural networks" (**Christian Szegedy et al., 2013**, ICLR 2014). Imperceptible perturbations to images flip the classifier with high confidence; a printed sticker on a stop sign makes a self-driving car's vision system read "speed limit 45" (**Eykholt et al., 2018** — the first physical-world robustness demonstration). Mitigations: adversarial training, certified robustness (smaller models with formal robustness bounds), defensive distillation.

**Poisoning attacks**: at training time, inject corrupted data that biases the model. **Backdoor attacks** specifically: the poisoned model behaves normally on benign inputs but misbehaves on inputs with a specific trigger (a small patch, a special character, a watermark). Biggio et al. (2012) introduced the formal poisoning framework; later work by **Chen et al. (2017)** showed targeted backdoors in neural networks with high fidelity. Mitigations: training data provenance, outlier detection, federated learning with secure aggregation.

**Extraction attacks**: query a deployed model heavily to extract the model itself (model stealing) or training data (membership inference). **Tramer et al. (2016)** — "Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs" — demonstrated that black-box API access suffices to clone a model. **Shokri et al. (2017)** formalized membership inference. Mitigations: rate limiting, output perturbation, query distribution monitoring, differential privacy in training.

The field is empirical — every defense has been broken by stronger attacks, and 2024-2025 attention has shifted from 'achieve robustness on a specific benchmark' to 'set up empirically defensible deployment with the right monitoring + rate-limiting controls'.

slides.title: FGSM, PGD, Carlini-Wagner: the attack taxonomy in depth
slides.body:
**Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)** — introduced by **Ian Goodfellow, Jonathon Shlens, and Christian Szegedy** in "Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples" (*ICLR 2015*, arXiv 2014). The perturbation is $\delta = \varepsilon \cdot \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_x L(x, y; \theta))$, the sign of the loss gradient scaled by $\varepsilon$. It is a **one-step** $\ell_\infty$-bounded attack — fast but weak.

**Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)** — introduced by **Aleksander Madry, Aleksandar Makelov, Ludwig Schmidt, Dimitris Tsipras, and Adrian Vladu** in "Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks" (*ICLR 2018*, arXiv 2017). PGD iterates FGSM with small steps $\alpha$ and projects back onto the $\varepsilon$-ball after each step:
$$x^{t+1} = \Pi_{B_\varepsilon(x)} \left( x^t + \alpha \cdot \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_x L) \right)$$
PGD is the **gold-standard attack** for evaluating robustness. **Madry et al.'s** key insight: training with PGD-generated adversarial examples ("PGD adversarial training") achieves a saddle-point solution to a minimax problem — the most principled robustness training known.

**Carlini-Wagner (C&W) attacks** — **Nicholas Carlini and David Wagner**, "Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks: An Ensemble of Diverse Approaches" (*IEEE S&P 2017*). C&W reformulates adversarial example generation as a constrained optimisation problem, finding the **minimum-norm** perturbation sufficient to cause misclassification. C&W attacks broke several proposed defenses (including defensive distillation) that had appeared promising against FGSM/PGD. Their paper is also notable as a methodological contribution: it introduced a rigorous framework for evaluating robustness claims.

**Certified robustness + randomized smoothing**: Formal guarantees that no adversarial example exists within a ball around a given input. **Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter ("Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing", ICML 2019)** showed that smoothing a classifier by adding Gaussian noise and taking the majority vote gives a provably robust classifier with $\ell_2$ radius guarantees. The tradeoff: certified radius is small and clean accuracy drops.

**The transferability property** (first noted by Szegedy et al. 2013, systematically studied by **Papernot, McDaniel, and Goodfellow, 2016**): an adversarial example crafted for model $M_1$ often fools model $M_2$ even with different architecture and training data. Transferability means **security through API obscurity fails** — an attacker can craft attacks on a surrogate model.

slides.title: Adversarial examples, transferability + the LLM frontier
slides.body:
An adversarial example for image classifier $M_1$ often *also* fools classifier $M_2$ even if $M_2$ was trained on different data with a different architecture. This **transferability** — systematic study by **Papernot et al. (2016)** and **Liu et al., "Delving into Transferable Adversarial Examples and Black-box Attacks" (ICLR 2017)** — exploits shared structure of learned decision boundaries across models.

Consequence: an attacker without API access to your deployed model can craft adversarial examples on a *surrogate* model and they will likely transfer. 'Security through API obscurity' doesn't work.

**Adversarial training** (**Madry et al., 2017/2018**): include PGD-generated adversarial examples in the training set. This solves a minimax problem: $\min_\theta \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)} \left[ \max_{\delta \in B_\varepsilon} L(x+\delta, y; \theta) \right]$. Robust models trained this way exhibit a known **accuracy-robustness tradeoff** — clean accuracy drops by a few percentage points; robustness against PGD-style attacks improves substantially. **Tsipras et al. ("Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy", ICLR 2019)** showed this tradeoff is fundamental, not an artifact of training procedure.

**Data poisoning on LLMs**: **Wallace et al. (2021)** demonstrated that injecting a small number of poisoned training examples into a language model's fine-tuning set could cause targeted misbehavior. **Prompt injection attacks** (distinct from adversarial examples for vision) were catalogued systematically by **Perez and Ribeiro (2022)** — untrusted text in the context window that overrides system instructions. **Indirect prompt injection** (Greshake et al., 2023) showed that an attacker controlling a webpage or document a retrieval-augmented LLM fetches can hijack the model's actions.

For LLMs, **jailbreaking** (user tries to bypass safety fine-tuning) and **prompt injection** (external content contains hidden instructions) are the dominant adversarial attack classes. **Universal adversarial suffixes** (**Zou et al., "Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models", 2023**) showed that a fixed token suffix, found by gradient-based optimization, can reliably jailbreak multiple aligned LLMs. Defense in depth, monitoring, rate limiting, and sandboxed tool execution are the practical mitigations — the same architectural principles that apply to any adversarial setting.

question.question: Derive the FGSM perturbation
question.goal: Given input $x$ + loss $L(x, y; \theta)$, FGSM perturbation: $\delta = \epsilon \text{sign}(\nabla_x L)$.

steps.prompt: We want a small perturbation $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_\infty \leq \epsilon$ that maximally increases the loss. Linearize $L$ around $x$: $L(x + \delta) \approx L(x) + \nabla_x L \cdot \delta$. Maximize $\nabla_x L \cdot \delta$ subject to $\|\delta\|_\infty \leq \epsilon$.
steps.reveal: $\delta = \epsilon \text{sign}(\nabla_x L)$ — sign of the gradient, scaled by $\epsilon$.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\delta_{\text{FGSM}} = \epsilon \text{sign}(\nabla_x L)}$$ Fast Gradient Sign Method (Goodfellow 2014). One-step attack. PGD (Projected Gradient Descent) iterates FGSM with small steps + projection back to the $\epsilon$-ball — stronger attack, modern benchmark.

question.question: Adversarial examples for image classifiers usually look:
options: Indistinguishable to humans from the original.
question.explanation: Adversarial examples (in the vision-classifier literature) are usually constructed under $\epsilon$-ball constraints in pixel space — perturbations small enough to be visually imperceptible. The classifier flips its prediction confidently; the human can't see why. This is one of the more startling demonstrations in modern ML; the perturbations exploit the high-dimensional curvature of learned decision boundaries.

hints: Adversarial examples are usually crafted within an $\epsilon$-ball constraint in the input space.
slides.workedSolution: Standard adversarial examples are crafted to perturb the input by at most $\epsilon$ in $\ell_\infty$ norm — every pixel changes by at most $\epsilon$ (typically $\epsilon = 8/255$ for ImageNet). These perturbations are visually imperceptible; the classifier confidently changes its prediction. This is the canonical demonstration that learned classifiers have 'wrong' decision boundaries in adversarial directions even when they're accurate on clean data.

question.question: Prompt injection vs jailbreak
question.prompt: A user-facing LLM-based agent has tools to read files and send emails. A teammate distinguishes 'jailbreak' (user tries to make the model misbehave) from 'prompt injection' (untrusted content the model processes contains hidden instructions). Walk through which class is more dangerous in this deployment, and one defense for each.
Explain in two or three sentences why 'robust to all attacks' is provably impossible for any non-trivial ML model.
question.rubric: Mentions that the curse of dimensionality means adversarial directions exist in every input neighborhood; formal robustness can be proven only against specific bounded attack models; threat-model-specific defenses + monitoring + rate limiting are the practical answer.
